screens.title: Passing Data Between Activities
screens.subtitle: Use Intent extras to send values and objects when you navigate between screens

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on a practical skill you will use on almost every multi-screen Android app: sending information from one activity to another. You’ll learn how Intent objects can carry keyed data, why keys should be constants, and how to retrieve values safely on the receiving screen. We use real examples: sending a typed message or a small user object from MainActivity to SecondActivity, and we practice safe retrieval with default values and null checks. This matters because an app that navigates without passing the right data will show empty screens or crash. You’ll see concrete code patterns for putExtra and getStringExtra, and we’ll compare Parcelable and Serializable for moving custom objects. Throughout, I’ll point out common mistakes like key typos and wrong get-methods and show how to avoid them. By the end of the lesson you’ll be able to add an EditText, attach the entered name to an Intent, and read it back safely. Think about a list of items: what minimal data does the detail screen need? That question will guide the exercises we do next.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Intent extras are key-value pairs used to pass data between activities; always use consistent keys and retrieve values with a matching get...Extra method and safe defaults.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to package common data types and small objects into an Intent and reconstruct them in the destination activity. First, you will learn putExtra methods: how to attach Strings, numbers, and booleans using a unique string key so the receiving activity can find them. Second, you will learn the matching get... Extra retrieval methods like getStringExtra and getIntExtra, and how to provide safe default values or null checks to prevent crashes. Third, you will understand the concept of key-value pairs and why defining keys as constants avoids the common typo that leads to a null result. Finally, you will see two options for complex objects — Parcelable for performance and Serializable for simplicity — and when to prefer one over the other. Each objective is paired with a small visual mnemonic to help you remember the pattern and a verified competency milestone so you know when you’ve practiced it successfully.

screens.title: Intent Extras and Key-Value Pairs
screens.subtitle: Understand how extras package data inside an Intent

narration.text: An Intent is not just a navigation instruction; it is also a carrier for small pieces of data called extras. Extras are attached as key-value pairs: a string key uniquely identifies the value, which can be a String, Int, Boolean, Float, or an object like a Parcelable. Think of the key as the label on a folder and the value as the file inside. Using keys consistently is essential; a typo will mean the receiving activity cannot find the file and will get null or a default. A helpful mental model is a dictionary: keys map to values. For practice, imagine a list screen that sends an itemId to a detail screen — the detail activity reads the itemId and loads content for that id. A common misconception is to assume putExtra copies all app state — it does not. Extras are meant for small, explicit data needed by the destination. Large datasets should be stored in a shared repository or database and referenced by ID. To check your understanding, ask: what minimal piece of data does the target activity need to render its UI? That answer will become your key-value pair.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Extras are key-value pairs attached to an Intent to send small pieces of data to another activity.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Intent Extras
What is an extra?

A small piece of data attached to an Intent as a key-value pair. Keys are strings; values are typed.

Mnemonic
Think dictionary entry: key maps to value you need on the next screen.
Common types supported:
  • String, Int, Boolean, Float
  • Parcelable or Serializable objects for custom types
Key takeaway
Keep extras minimal and explicit; send the smallest data needed to render the next screen.
Concrete example

MainActivity sends an item id to DetailActivity so the detail screen fetches and shows the correct item.

Scenario
A shopping app passes productId=42 to the product screen, which then loads the product details from a repository.
Key Takeaway

Extras are ideal for passing small, explicit data that the next activity requires to render its UI.

Common mistake
Trying to pass large datasets via extras instead of using a shared data source or ID reference.

screens.title: Attaching Data with putExtra()
screens.subtitle: How to add typed extras to an Intent

narration.text: Attaching data to an Intent is a simple process but requires precision. First, decide on a unique key string and preferably define it as a constant so both activities use the exact same identifier. Second, get or compute the value you need to send, such as a name or an id. Third, create an Intent for the destination activity and call putExtra with the key and value. Android provides overloads so you can pass different types directly. Finally, call startActivity with the Intent. A concrete example: read the text from an EditText, build an Intent to SecondActivity, and call putExtra(USER_NAME_KEY, name). The process is straightforward but easy to break by using a literal key in one place and a constant in another, or by using the wrong put variant for the intended type. To check correctness, ensure that the receiving activity uses the same key string and a matching get method. This flow keeps data explicit and the navigation predictable. Attaching Data with putExtra() means define a key constant, compute value, call intent.putextra(key, value), then startactivity(intent).. In practical terms, how to add typed extras to an intent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: putExtra flow
keyIdea.text: Define a key constant, compute value, call intent.putExtra(key, value), then startActivity(intent).

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › putExtra()
Step-by-step
  1. Define a constant key string to avoid typos.
  2. Read or compute the value to send (text, id, boolean).
  3. Create an Intent to the destination activity.
  4. Call putExtra(key, value) with the appropriate type overload.
  5. Start the activity with startActivity(intent).
Example outcome
When you call putExtra with a String, the destination can use getStringExtra with the same key to retrieve it.
Code example
// In MainActivity.kt
const val USER_NAME_KEY = "com.example.mymultiscreenapp.USER_NAME"

// inside onCreate()
val nameInputEditText: EditText = findViewById(R.id.name_input_edit_text)
val goToSecondButton: Button = findViewById(R.id.btn_go_to_second)

goToSecondButton.setOnClickListener {
  val userName = nameInputEditText.text.toString()
  val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java).apply {
    putExtra(USER_NAME_KEY, userName)
  }
  startActivity(intent)
}
Key Takeaway

Always use a constant key and the matching putExtra overload for the value type you intend to send.

screens.title: Retrieving Data with get...Extra()
screens.subtitle: How to read extras safely in the destination activity

narration.text: Reading extras properly is as important as adding them. The Intent that started an activity carries any attached extras and you retrieve them using the corresponding get method. For Strings use getStringExtra, for integers use getIntExtra which requires a default, and for booleans use getBooleanExtra with a default value. Because getStringExtra returns a nullable String, handle nulls with the Elvis operator to provide a fallback. An example pattern is val name = intent. getStringExtra(USER_NAME_KEY)?: "Guest". A common pitfall is using the wrong get method for the type you put, or assuming getStringExtra returns a non-null result. Also note that getIntExtra requires an explicit default value like 0; if the key is missing the default is returned. To verify correctness, simulate a missing extra and ensure your app shows the fallback rather than crashing. Practice reading different types, and always think about what sensible default the UI should show if no value was passed. Retrieving Data with get...Extra() means use matching get methods and provide defaults or null-safe fallbacks to avoid crashes when extras are missing.. In practical terms, how to read extras safely in the destination activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe retrieval
keyIdea.text: Use matching get methods and provide defaults or null-safe fallbacks to avoid crashes when extras are missing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › get...Extra()
Core retrieval patterns
  • getStringExtra returns a nullable String; use ?: for a default.
  • getIntExtra and getBooleanExtra require a default parameter to return when key is missing.
  • Use the exact same key string used for putExtra to retrieve the value.
Misconception
Assuming getStringExtra never returns null leads to crashes when you dereference without a fallback.
Key Takeaway

Always provide a default or null-safe fallback when reading extras.

Code walkthrough
// In SecondActivity.kt
// Assume USER_NAME_KEY is accessible
class SecondActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
  override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_second)

    val displayNameTextView: TextView = findViewById(R.id.display_name_text_view)

    val userName = intent.getStringExtra(USER_NAME_KEY) ?: "Guest"
    displayNameTextView.text = "Hello, $${'{' }userName}${'}'}!"
  }
}
Try this: remove the extra in the sender and confirm SecondActivity shows the fallback text instead of crashing.

screens.title: Keys as Constants vs Literal Strings
screens.subtitle: Avoid hard-to-find bugs by centralizing keys

narration.text: A tiny difference in a key string can become a frustrating bug. If you use a literal string in one activity and a different literal elsewhere, the receiving activity will not find the extra and you’ll see null or default values without an immediate crash, which makes the bug subtle. The recommended approach is to define your intent keys as top-level constants so both sender and receiver import or reference the same value. This reduces typos and makes refactoring safer. Another benefit is discoverability: constants give meaningful names and make it clear where keys are defined. A common misconception is that defining a key in multiple classes as identical text is safe; it is only safe when the text is actually identical. Using a single constant avoids accidental mismatches. For modular code or feature modules, consider housing key constants near the data type or in a shared constants file so consumers can import them reliably. Keys as Constants vs Literal Strings means define intent extra keys as constants and reuse them across activities to avoid typos and subtle bugs.. In practical terms, avoid hard-to-find bugs by centralizing keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Best practice
keyIdea.text: Define intent extra keys as constants and reuse them across activities to avoid typos and subtle bugs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Key Constants
Why constants?

Constants keep a single source of truth for key strings and make your code easier to maintain and refactor.

Pattern
Define a top-level constant near your activity or in a shared file, then reference it from both sender and receiver.
Mistake to avoid
Using different literal strings in sender and receiver; the mismatch returns null silently.
Quick example
const val USER_NAME_KEY = "com.example.mymultiscreenapp.USER_NAME"
Developer tip

Group keys logically and name them with a package-like prefix to reduce accidental collisions.

screens.title: Parcelable vs Serializable
screens.subtitle: Choose the right approach for passing custom objects

narration.text: When you need to pass a custom object between activities, Android offers two common approaches: Parcelable and Serializable. Parcelable is an Android-specific interface optimized for performance; it requires you to implement how the object is written to and restored from a parcel. Modern Kotlin tooling often generates much of this code automatically through the kotlin-parcelize plugin, which makes Parcelable convenient and efficient. Serializable is a standard Java interface that is easier to implement — often just marking the class as Serializable — but it is less efficient because it uses reflection and can allocate more memory. For small apps or small objects, Serializable may be acceptable, but for performance-sensitive paths Parcelable is preferred. A common misconception is that Serializable is always simpler and therefore always fine; in Android, for objects passed frequently or with many fields, Parcelable usually performs better. Consider object size, frequency of transfer, and tooling support when choosing between them. Parcelable vs Serializable means parcelable is more efficient on android but requires more setup; serializable is simpler but less performant.. In practical terms, choose the right approach for passing custom objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Parcelable is more efficient on Android but requires more setup; Serializable is simpler but less performant.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Parcelable vs Serializable
Parcelable

Android-optimized interface for writing objects to and restoring from a Parcel. Preferred for performance.

When to use
Use Parcelable when objects are passed frequently or performance matters.
Serializable

Standard Java serialization. Simpler to implement but less efficient on Android due to reflection.

When to use
Acceptable for small apps or rarely passed objects where convenience outweighs performance.
Key Takeaway

Prefer Parcelable for Android apps when performance matters; use Serializable for simplicity in low-cost cases.

screens.title: Parcelable Example with @Parcelize
screens.subtitle: A practical Kotlin data class that is parcelable

narration.text: Kotlin provides a concise way to make data classes parcelable using the kotlin-parcelize plugin and the @Parcelize annotation. The basic idea is to mark the class with the annotation and implement Parcelable in the class header, and the compiler will generate the parceling code for you. A simple User data class with id, name, and email fields works well as an example. Once you have a parcelable object, you can call putExtra with the object and retrieve it in the destination using getParcelableExtra. Remember to keep parcelable objects reasonably small and focused: avoid referencing large UI state or heavy resources. A common misconception is that @Parcelize removes all complexity; it helps a lot, but you must still ensure the class fields themselves are parcelable or primitive types. After creating the parcelable, test sending and retrieving it, and handle the null case in the receiver to avoid unexpected failures. Parcelable Example with @Parcelize means use @parcelize on a kotlin data class and implement parcelable to pass custom objects via intent extras.. In practical terms, a practical kotlin data class that is parcelable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Parcelize pattern
keyIdea.text: Use @Parcelize on a Kotlin data class and implement Parcelable to pass custom objects via Intent extras.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › @Parcelize Example
Data class example
// User.kt
import android.os.Parcelable
import kotlinx.parcelize.Parcelize

@Parcelize
data class User(val id: Int, val name: String, val email: String) : Parcelable
This class can now be attached to an Intent with putExtra("USER_DATA", user) and restored with getParcelableExtra.
Send and receive
// Sending
val user = User(1, "Alice", "alice@example.com")
val intent = Intent(this, SecondActivity::class.java).apply {
  putExtra("USER_DATA", user)
}
startActivity(intent)

// Receiving
val user: User? = intent.getParcelableExtra("USER_DATA")
if (user != null) {
  receivedMessageTextView.text = "Welcome, ${'${'}user.name${'}'}!"
} else {
  receivedMessageTextView.text = "No user data received."
}
Tip: Make sure the same key string is used when sending and receiving. Consider defining it as a constant to avoid typos.

screens.title: Retrieving Complex Objects & Casting
screens.subtitle: Use getParcelableExtra and handle nulls and casts safely

narration.text: When you retrieve a parcelable or serializable object from an Intent, you must use the matching retrieval method and treat the result as nullable. For parcelable objects call getParcelableExtra with the key and assign it to a nullable reference of your custom type. Then check for null before using the object. For serializable objects use getSerializableExtra and cast it to your type, remembering to handle the case where the cast fails or the extra is missing. A frequent mistake is to assume the object is present and directly access its fields without a null check, which can cause a crash. Another pitfall is using the wrong retrieval method, for example calling getStringExtra for an object; that will return null. A good pattern is to use a safe let or an if check: val user: User? = intent. getParcelableExtra("USER_DATA") ; user?. let { showName(it. name) }?: showNoUserMessage(). This keeps your UI robust and predictable. Retrieving Complex Objects & Casting means call the matching get method for your object type and always handle the nullable result before using fields or methods.. In practical terms, use getparcelableextra and handle nulls and casts safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe object retrieval
keyIdea.text: Call the matching get method for your object type and always handle the nullable result before using fields or methods.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Retrieve Objects
Pattern for parcelable
val user: User? = intent.getParcelableExtra("USER_DATA")
if (user != null) {
  // safe to use user.name
  showWelcome(user.name)
} else {
  showNoUserMessage()
}
Always treat retrieved objects as nullable and handle the missing case gracefully.
Pattern for serializable
val serial = intent.getSerializableExtra("USER_DATA")
val user = serial as? User
if (user != null) {
  showWelcome(user.name)
} else {
  showNoUserMessage()
}
Note: The safe cast operator as? avoids a ClassCastException if the extra is not the expected type.

screens.title: Common Errors and Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Debugging missing extras, type mismatches and casting issues

narration.text: When extras don’t appear as expected there are a few typical culprits to check. First, verify the key strings match exactly — a typo is the most common cause of missing extras. Second, ensure you’re using the correct get method for the type you sent; retrieving with the wrong getter returns null or a default. Third, ensure complex objects implement Parcelable or Serializable as expected and that you use getParcelableExtra or getSerializableExtra respectively. For cast failures, prefer safe casts that return null rather than throwing. Also check the lifecycle: make sure the code that reads intent extras runs after the activity is created, typically in onCreate. Use logging to print the contents of intent. extras to inspect what was sent. A misconception is assuming a missing extra causes a crash; often it silently returns null which can later cause a crash if you dereference it. The troubleshooting steps are: check keys, check types, add logging, and add null-safe handling. This process will quickly reveal where the mismatch or oversight happened. Common Errors and Troubleshooting means if an extra is missing, check keys, get method types, object interfaces, lifecycle timing, and inspect intent.extras via logging.. In practical terms, debugging missing extras, type mismatches and casting issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debug checklist
keyIdea.text: If an extra is missing, check keys, get method types, object interfaces, lifecycle timing, and inspect intent.extras via logging.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Troubleshooting
Checklist to find missing extras
  • Verify the exact key string is identical in sender and receiver.
  • Confirm you used the correct get...Extra method for the value type.
  • For objects, ensure they implement Parcelable or Serializable and you use the matching getter.
  • Check that retrieval code runs in onCreate after setContentView.
  • Log intent.extras to inspect what was actually sent.
Example log
Log.d("IntentExtras", intent.extras?.keySet()?.toString() ?: "no extras")
Pro tip

When debugging, temporarily display debugging text in the UI listing the extras so you can see them without scanning logs.

The correct answer is intent. putExtra("userId", 123) because putExtra takes a string key and a value. This mini-quiz reinforces the pattern: send with putExtra(key, value), retrieve with matching get method, and always provide a fallback. After these checks you should be confident the app handles both present and missing data robustly. narration.text: Let’s summarize the essential concepts to remember. First, Intent extras are key-value pairs used to pass small, explicit data between activities. Second, always use the appropriate putExtra and matching get... Extra methods for the data type you are sending, and provide defaults or null-safe fallbacks to avoid unexpected nulls. Third, prefer defining keys as constants to avoid typos that lead to missing data. These three practices together make multi-screen navigation robust and predictable. Use these reminders as a checklist when you build transitions: define a key constant, send the minimal required data, and read it back with safe defaults. narration.text: A few final reminders: Parcelable is the efficient Android way to serialize objects and is preferred for performance-sensitive transfers. Serializable is simpler but may be slower and allocate more memory. Always handle nullable returns when retrieving extras and choose sensible defaults for your UI. Finally, treat extras as a mechanism for small, explicit data; for larger datasets prefer shared storage or IDs passed by extras. Parcelable

Null Handling
Use the Elvis operator or defaults for nullable extras to ensure stable UI behavior.
Keep Extras Small
Pass IDs or minimal fields; use shared storage for large datasets.
